title: Three-by-Three Peak Map
statement:
You get an n × n integer grid grid. Slide a 3 × 3 window over every position where it fits completely inside the grid.

Return an (n − 2) × (n − 2) grid out where out[i][j] is the largest value inside the window whose top-left cell is grid[i][j], i.e. rows i .. i + 2 and columns j .. j + 2.

examples.why: A 3 × 3 grid has exactly one window, and its largest value is 9.
The 5 at (1, 1) lies in all four windows, but the 7 in the corner lies only in the bottom-right one.
The 6 sits in row 0, column 3, so only the window starting at row 0, column 1 sees it. Mixing up rows and columns would swap the 6 and the 3.

gen: (r, big) => { const n = big ? 100 : r.int(3, 6); return [r.matrix(n, n, 1, big ? 100 : 9)]; }
hints: How many windows are there along one side? Their top-left corners run from 0 to n − 3.
For each top-left corner (i, j), the window covers rows i to i + 2 and columns j to j + 2.
Nine comparisons per window is constant work, so two loops over corners plus a fixed 3 × 3 inner scan is already linear in the grid size.

explain.intuition:
This is a 2D sliding window with a fixed size of 3, much like a blur or max-pool filter in image processing. Each output cell looks at a fixed 3 × 3 patch, so the direct approach does 9 comparisons per cell, which is already O(n²) overall.

A neat alternative splits the 2D max into two 1D passes: first take the max of every horizontal run of 3 in each row, then the max of every vertical run of 3 in those results. The max of a rectangle equals the max over its rows of each row's max, so the two passes give the same answer. This separability matters when the window is large.
steps: For each i and j from 0 to n − 3, scan grid[i + di][j + dj] for di, dj in 0..2.
Store the largest of those nine values in out[i][j].
pitfalls: Treating (i, j) as the centre of the window and reading from i − 1. The statement uses the top-left corner, which gives the same grid only if your indices shift by one everywhere.
Swapping rows and columns when filling the output. The third example catches this: the 6 and the 3 change places.
Looping corners up to n − 2 inclusive and reading past the edge.

solutions.title: Scan every 3 × 3 window
solutions.idea: For each top-left corner, look at the nine cells and keep the maximum.

solutions.title: Separable max: rows, then columns
solutions.idea: First take the max of each horizontal triple in every row, then the max of each vertical triple of those values.

followups: The window is k × k instead of 3 × 3. How do you keep the work O(n²) regardless of k? (Monotonic deque per row, then per column.)
Return the window sums instead of maxima. Which precomputation makes each sum O(1)?
lcTitle: Largest Local Values in a Matrix
